newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians skilled at bypass, Yeltsin may need more.
newsitem.headline: Russians skilled at bypass, Yeltsin may need more.

text.p: A small but highly competent band of Russian doctors is very capable of carrying out the fairly routine heart bypass surgery that specialists say Boris Yeltsin plans to have later this month.
But details of the operation, announced by the president on Thursday in a novel gesture of televised candour, are hazy.

Leading Russian cardiologist Valery Sadrikov told Interfax news agency on Friday that Yeltsin would have a heart bypass to correct ischaemia -- a lack of blood flowing to the heart. This condition put the president in hospital twice last year.
Yet some experts say his illness may be less straightforward than Kremlin spin doctors would have the world believe.
Sadrikov said Yeltsin would have the bypass operation at Moscow's Cardiological Centre, headed by Yevgeny Chazov. The president had indicated on Thursday that this was his choice.
Chazov, however, told Interfax he did not know where the president planned to have surgery or what it involved.

But the world-renowned expert who kept Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev alive for almost a decade of hushed-up decline did confirm that Yeltsin had undergone tests at his clinic, close to the president's apartment in a southwest Moscow suburb.
Many of Chazov's surgeons have trained in the United States.
A Kremlin source had told Reuters on Thursday that relatively routine bypass surgery was more than likely.
Mikhail Alshibaya, a surgeon at the capital's Scientific Centre for Cardiovascular Surgery, told Ekho Moskvy radio Russia had the expertise to perform it as well as in western clinics.
A bypass typically means grafting a vein from the patient's leg or elsewhere to divert blood past the blockage to the heart.

"It's a pretty routine and safe operation," John Walwark, director of transplant surgery at Britain's pioneering heart clinic at Papworth Hospital, Cambridge, said. He put the chances of dying from the operation at around two percent.
Hundreds of thousands are performed in the West every year.
Alshibaya said no more than 5,000 bypass treatments were done in Russia annually by a group of surgeons "you could count on your fingers". But they were as skilled as those in the West.

"They do a huge number of such operations and their results do not differ significantly from the West. The difference is limited to the level of equipment and availability of medicines. But this does not apply to the president of Russia," he said.
Western doctors working in Moscow also said they did not doubt Russia had the necessary specialists for bypass surgery.

Transplant specialist Mikhail Semyonovsky told Interfax that the bulk of these "common and banal" bypass operations in Russia were carried out in four Moscow clinics. Patients were usually restored to an active life after about a month of convalescence.
"He should really have a good chance of a good recovery," Walwark said. "Unless there are other complications that we are not privy too."
Precisely this question of "complications" will remain to the fore as Yeltsin prepares to go under the knife.

One leading European neurosurgeon, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters that Yeltsin's apparently limited power of movement down his left side indicated he may have a blood clot on his brain -- in other words, he has had a mild stroke.
A western cardiologist, who declined to be named, said she had detected sounds indicating the president also had water on his lungs during some of his recent appearances.
That, she said, suggested trouble with the heart's left ventricle and could mean more drastic -- and risky -- surgery.
With the bulk of the political power in Russia's still fledgling democracy concentrated in the hands of the ailing president, such doubts will worry many beyond its borders.
